title: The Partridge and the Fowler
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Fowler caught a Partridge in his nets, and was just about to wring its neck when it made a piteous appeal to him to spare its life and said, "Do not kill me, but let me live and I will repay you for your kindness by decoying other partridges into your nets." "No," said the Fowler, "I will not spare you. I was going to kill you anyhow, and after that treacherous speech you thoroughly deserve your fate."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Fowler catch the Partridge?
options: In his nets
With a trap
With his bare hands
With a snare made of vine

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Fowler just about to do when the Partridge spoke?
options: Release it into the wild
Sell it at the market
Feed it some grain
Wring its neck

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Partridge promise to do if its life were spared?
options: Lead the Fowler to a hidden treasure
Teach the Fowler how to hunt better
Decoy other partridges into the Fowler's nets
Give the Fowler one of its feathers each year

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fowler respond to the Partridge's plea?
options: He agrees at once
He refuses to spare it
He hesitates and asks for time to think
He sets it free without conditions

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "piteous" mean in "made a piteous appeal"?
options: Arrogant and demanding
Evoking pity or sorrow
Loud and angry
Brief and businesslike

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "treacherous" mean in "that treacherous speech"?
options: Extremely clever
Frightened and timid
Disloyal or betraying trust
Boring and repetitive

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Fowler call the Partridge's offer "treacherous"?
options: The Partridge offered to betray other partridges of its own kind to save itself
The Partridge lied about being caught in a net
The Partridge insulted the Fowler's hunting skills
The Partridge tried to escape while speaking

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Fowlers should always spare animals that beg for their lives
Partridges are cleverer than fowlers
Nets are the most effective way to catch birds
One who offers to betray others to save itself deserves no mercy

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Partridge ask the Fowler to do?
options: Trade it for a different bird
Take it to another hunter
Not kill it, but let it live
Let it fly free immediately

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fowler say about his original plan for the Partridge?
options: He had already decided to spare it
He planned to sell it alive
He had not yet decided its fate
He was going to kill it anyhow

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "decoying" mean in "decoying other partridges into your nets"?
options: Luring or attracting into a trap
Feeding and caring for
Warning away from danger
Racing against

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "wring" mean in "wring its neck"?
options: To gently stroke
To measure carefully
To twist forcefully
To decorate

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Fowler's response reveal about how he judges the Partridge's character?
options: He admires the Partridge's cleverness and spares it
He believes the Partridge is telling the truth and trusts it fully
He thinks the Partridge is too weak to be dangerous
He sees its willingness to betray its own kind as making it even less deserving of mercy

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fowler frees a Partridge after it promises to help him hunt
A Partridge begs a Fowler for its life by offering to betray other partridges, but the Fowler kills it anyway, seeing the offer as further proof it deserves no mercy
A Partridge escapes the Fowler's nets on its own
A Fowler and a Partridge become hunting partners
